paragraphs: Glass Recycling to Foam-Glass Products – Detailed Business Plan
Document version: v1.0
Author: Tomas Svoboda
Scope: Concept / pre-FEED business and technical pack
Location: Curaçao

This document expands the initial concept note into a pre-FEED level business and technical plan. It is intentionally more conservative where real-world bottlenecks exist, especially around feedstock capture, usable waste heat, process water and island-specific execution risk.
Why?
Solving trouble with glass waste on the ABC islands
Creating locally necessary material for building construction
Creating new jobs and support economy during factory building (preferred local suppliers)
1. Executive framing

The project converts mixed waste glass from Curaçao (and ideal from Aruba and Bonaire too) into two core products: foam-glass aggregate and foam-glass blocks. The reference production concept is a 30 m electric tunnel kiln with annual output of about 19,162 m³/yr at 75% calendar utilization, equivalent to about 2,951 t/yr of finished product.

The central strategic logic is import substitution and waste reduction. The plant does not need enormous tonnage to operate. In the base case it needs only about 3,451 t/yr of mixed raw glass at the factory gate. That is small enough to be plausible on Curaçao, but large enough that it still requires deliberate collection contracts rather than passive assumptions.
Three corrections materially change the economics compared with an optimistic first-pass concept:

The kiln's recoverable low-grade heat should not be valued as if 150–250 kW can always be consumed. In the base case the realistic wash + dry thermal sink is only about 159 MWhth/yr on average, or roughly 73 kWth if the wash line runs one 8-hour shift.
Dedicated desalination is not justified for phase 1. Process make-up water is only about 248 m³/yr, so buying industrial water is cheaper and far simpler if a utility connection exists.

A battery should be justified primarily by resilience, power-quality support and operating flexibility, not by energy arbitrage. The current industrial high/low tariff spread is too small for a pure tariff-arbitrage case.
Finances

CAPEX is in basic version of plan 19,600,000 USD, but it can be optimized 17,600,000 USD by splitting some investments into next phases of project without affecting start of the project. CAPEX must be considered over time (project contains building constructions, large technologies => spread over 1-2y).
OPEX total revenue is modeled between 3,7-4,4mil.USD based on scenario. Main items on expenses side are:
Payroll: 1mil.USD (30 FTE)
Grid electricity: 0.48mil.USD
Maintenance: 0.25mil.USD
Collection and transport: 0.24mil.USD
Other: 0.6-0.8mil.USD

Realistic pure possible payback of investment is between 12-15 years. It does not consider other efects on local economy, that cretes huge additional value such as decrease need for concrete, free up areas for storing glass waste, back investment to local economy during building factory, creating new jobs and other non-financial aspects. Project is not suitable for pure financial investor, but great profitable step for government.
2. What the plant will make and why it should exist
The plant will manufacture two foam-glass product families from mixed bottle and flat-glass waste:

Foam-glass aggregate: 11,498 m³/yr in the base case. This is the lower-finishing, easier-to-place product. It is relevant for lightweight fill, drainage layers, sub-base, roof build-ups and insulating fill.
Foam-glass blocks / bricks: 7,665 m³/yr in the base case. This product commands a higher selling price but requires stricter process control, cutting, trimming and pallet handling.
Foam-glass blocks/slabs Foam-glass aggregate / gravel

A dual-product strategy is important on an island. Aggregate gives a broad local outlet and tolerates a slightly wider process window. Blocks create margin and visibility, but they should not be the only route to market. The recommended starting mix is 60% aggregate and 40% blocks by volume, with the option to flex after market testing.

The plant should not be treated as a generic recycling line. It is a specialty thermal-processing plant that happens to use waste glass as feedstock. That means the real value drivers are recipe stability, thermal control, capture logistics, and local market realization rather than the mere fact that a kiln exists.
Figure 1. Detailed process flow used for the base concept.
3. Demand and market logic

The local business case depends on replacing imported lightweight fill and insulation materials whose delivered island cost is elevated by freight, handling and inventory. That is why the plan deliberately uses local selling-price ranges rather than mainland commodity assumptions.

In the base scenario the model uses 165 USD/m³ for aggregate and 240 USD/m³ for blocks. These are not 'guaranteed' market prices, with actual geopolitical situation you can expect large inflation in next years. Same as price of the sand usable in concrete, that increase demand for fillings that can be used in concrete (for example glass foam). They are planning values that still need confirmation by contractor interviews, pilot samples and delivered-import benchmarking.

The right commercial posture is not 'cheap recycled material'. It is 'local engineered lightweight insulation / fill with lower logistics friction, shorter lead time and visible environmental value'. The nearer the project gets to construction and hospitality buyers, the more defensible the product premium becomes.
Anchor customers should include civil contractors, roofing and waterproofing contractors, resort and hotel owners, developers, and public infrastructure programs.
At least 70% of base output should be covered by anchor offtake before final investment approval. The plant should not rely on discovering the market after commissioning.
Export to nearby islands can be opportunistic, but the base project should stand on Curaçao demand plus only modest export flexibility.
Figure 2. EBITDA sensitivity across conservative, base and upside operating envelopes.
4. Feedstock strategy and can the island really support the plant?

The plant's base mixed-glass requirement is about 3,451 t/yr. This is the single most important physical constraint because the kiln prefers continuous operation and because feedstock shortfall is much harder to fix later than payroll or packaging cost.

There is no reliable single official number in the project pack that proves, by itself, that Curaçao already delivers this exact quantity of clean and capturable mixed glass. Therefore the project should be framed honestly: feedstock sufficiency must be demonstrated by a capture model plus signed contracts, not by wishful top-down waste percentages.
The most practical approach is a bottom-up capture model built from four streams:
Residents and retail drop-off.
Stayover tourism / HORECA (hotels, bars, restaurants, resorts).
Construction and demolition flat glass from windows and renovation.
Optional neighboring-island top-up only as a buffer, not the primary business case.
Table 1. Modeled capturable mixed-glass envelope (planning assumption, not official waste statistics).

The modeled base capture case reaches about 3,592 t/yr, which is only modestly above the base plant need of 3,451 t/yr. That is simultaneously encouraging and a warning. It means the plant is not absurdly oversized for the island, but it also means execution has to be disciplined. A weak collection program could easily underfeed the plant. Those numbers are just for Curaçao. It would be good to consider collection of glass from Aruba and Bonaire too. If all islands will participate, it would be possible to increase the capacity of the plant, that can lead to better EBIDTA.

A sensible pre-FID target is therefore at least 4.0–4.2 kt/yr of contracted mixed-glass supply, leaving some margin above modeled base need. That contract basket should combine municipal / partner collection, hotel and resort contracts, and construction-window recovery.

A separate sense-check also helps. Beer imports alone are large enough to indicate that beverage packaging flow is meaningful on the island, even though not all of that volume is in recoverable glass bottles. The purpose of that benchmark is not to prove the exact answer, but to confirm that the plant's 3.45 kt/yr requirement is not outlandish in scale.
Figure 3. Modeled base feedstock segments compared with raw-glass need.
5. Collection and transport logistics

Collection design matters more than people often expect. Because the plant's annual feedstock need is moderate rather than massive, it is usually smarter to optimize routing, consolidation and contamination control than to overinvest in a large owned fleet on day one.
Table 2. Base-case logistics quantities.

The practical implication is straightforward. If all hotel / bar material were delivered directly to the plant by small route trucks, the model implies roughly 986 loaded trips per year, or a little over three loaded routes per collection day. If glass is first consolidated into a central transfer point and then line-hauled to the plant in 7 t loads, that falls to roughly 493 loaded factory-inbound trips per year.

For that reason, the reference design assumes the core plant is built without a full islandwide self-owned collection fleet. Instead, collection is handled by partner routes, a municipal interface, outsourced transport, or a later optional fleet add-on. The factory's core economics should not be burdened with a fully in-house route network before the feedstock basin is proven.

Sea logistics should remain optional. The former refinery setting makes marine access attractive, but the base business case should not rely on inter-island shipping. Marine top-up is best used as contingency capacity after local collection is functioning.
Figure 4. Concept site masterplan on a former refinery parcel.
6. Process and technology basis
The chosen flow sheet is intentionally conventional rather than exotic. That improves serviceability and de-risks spare parts on an island:
Receiving, stockpiling and pre-sort.
Mechanical separation: trommel / screens, ferrous and non-ferrous metal removal, optical sorting.
Wash, rinse, dryer and recirculating water loop with filter-press sludge handling.
Coarse crushing and fine milling to glass flour.
Silos, gravimetric dosing and intensive mixing with a foaming package and process aids.
Forming and continuous passage through a 30 m electric tunnel kiln.
Controlled cooling and split into two finishing streams: block trimming / palletizing and aggregate crushing / bagging.

The recipe is still a pilot-trial matter, not a fixed procurement list. For concept modeling, it is enough to assume that purchased additives equal about 2.5% of clean-glass mass. That package can include the foaming agent itself plus one or more process aids. The plant should not commit to a final additive package until real Curaçao cullet blends are tested, especially because flat-glass fractions can shift viscosity and foaming behavior.
The base material balance indicates 2,968 t/yr of clean glass plus 74 t/yr of additives to produce 2,951 t/yr of finished foam-glass products.
Table 3. Base material balance.

The tunnel kiln is modeled as a 1 MW connected load with a lower average operating draw in steady production. This distinction matters. If the kiln truly averaged 1 MW continuously all year, the specific energy intensity would be too high relative to benchmark foam-glass processes. The planning model therefore treats 1 MW as installed/available capacity and about 550 kW as a realistic base running draw during stable production.
Figure 5. Internal hall arrangement showing the planned west-to-east material flow.
7. Energy model and why the 'waste heat' story must stay realistic
Total base-case plant electricity is modeled at about 4,052 MWh/yr or 211.4 kWh/m³. Of that, the kiln itself is about 3,614 MWh/yr and auxiliaries about 438 MWh/yr.
Table 4. Base-case electricity load breakdown.

Own renewable generation from 1 MWp PV and 200 kW wind is modeled at about 2,496 MWh/yr, of which roughly 2,296 MWh/yr is self-consumed on site. Grid import remains material at about 1,756 MWh/yr, which is why grid quality and backup strategy still matter.

The essential insight is that heat recovery must be matched to a real thermal sink. The initial concept note discussed much larger annual savings from 150–250 kW of recovered heat. That is not supported by the wash/dry duty actually required for this plant.

In the base case, wash and dry together need only about 159 MWhth/yr. If the wash line ran in a single 8-hour daily shift, that equates to roughly 72.7 kWth average thermal demand during the shift. That is useful, but it is far below a continuously usable 150–250 kW recovery case.
This changes design decisions immediately:
A modest heat-recovery loop is justified.
A small hot-water buffer is justified to decouple the kiln from wash scheduling.
A very large thermal store is not justified unless a second heat customer exists on site.
Projected savings must be capped by actual heat consumption, not by theoretical recoverable exhaust heat.

A 20 m³ hot-water buffer at a 35°C working temperature spread stores about 0.81 MWhth and is adequate to shift more than one operating day of wash/dry demand. A 70 m³ store would be materially oversized unless another process or neighboring plant bought the heat.
Figure 6. Energy, water and resilience schematic used for the base concept.
Figure 7. Base-case electricity balance between on-site renewables and grid import.
8. Water, desalination and seawater cooling

Gross wash-loop circulation is modeled at about 1,381 m³/yr, but with 82% recycle the fresh make-up requirement is only about 248 m³/yr. At current industrial-water tariffs this is a minor annual cost item rather than a capex driver.
Table 5. Base-case water balance.

This leads to a strong design conclusion: a dedicated SWRO desalination plant should not be part of phase 1 unless industrial water is unavailable or extremely unreliable. The process simply does not consume enough fresh water for a stand-alone desalination system to earn its keep.

The same logic applies to seawater cooling. It may become attractive later if the broader industrial parcel develops shared utility infrastructure, but it is not required by the base foam-glass process case. Including it too early only dilutes capital efficiency.

The correct phase-1 water strategy is utility water connection, recirculation, sludge handling, and right-sized buffer tankage. Only after actual plant operation is understood should optional SWRO or seawater loops be revisited as part of a broader site-wide utility strategy.
9. Electrical resilience, battery role and diesel backup

The electrical system should be designed as an industrial-quality micro-system embedded in the wider grid rather than as a standalone islanded plant. The main reasons are kiln continuity, harmonic management, and fast response to grid disturbances.

The 1 MW / 2 MWh battery gives roughly 3.6 h of autonomy against the kiln's modeled running average load, and about 6.7 h of autonomy against a 300 kW hot-hold essential-load case. That makes it valuable for ride-through, controlled load reduction and black-start support while the diesel generator starts or the grid recovers.
The battery should therefore be justified on four grounds:
ride-through during brief grid events;
fast load shaping and possible participation in system balancing;
smoother self-consumption of PV generation;
support for a controlled rather than chaotic response to outages.
What the battery should not be sold as is a classic time-of-use arbitrage machine. The tariff spread between industrial high and low periods is too small to justify that story on its own.
Table 6. Storage and resilience checks.
10. Site, buildings and brownfield reality

Using a former refinery parcel is strategically attractive. It offers industrial zoning logic, likely heavy-utility corridors, truck access and marine interface potential. But brownfields are never 'free'. They shift cost from greenfield civils into diligence, environmental management and uncertainty.

The reference site plan assumes a planning area of roughly four hectares. That allows a process hall, receiving yard, warehouse/dispatch zone, utility yard, PV area, truck circulation and a small future expansion strip without forcing an overly tight layout.

The real pre-FID gating item is not land size but site condition. Environmental baseline, geotechnical checks, drainage routing, stormwater handling, and existing buried services can all materially change civils cost. For that reason, the capex model carries dedicated brownfield survey / permitting cost and a meaningful contingency.
Do not commit to a specific plot before a desk environmental review and at least preliminary intrusive surveys.
Preserve one-way truck circulation and product dispatch space from the beginning; do not let energy assets consume the best logistics zones.
Treat corrosion and salt exposure as design-basis issues, not afterthoughts.
11. Staffing and operating model

The staffing plan is deliberately light but not 'indie'. It assumes basic industrial discipline, limited robotics and a process that still needs human supervision and maintenance. The core plant plan excludes a large self-owned route-collection organization, which can remain outsourced or partnered.
Table 7. Indicative core staffing plan.

The core staffing plan totals 30 FTE and roughly 1,025,892 USD/yr of loaded payroll. That is materially higher than a hand-wavy low-headcount concept, but it is much more defendable for a 24/7 thermal process on an island.

Shift structure should place the kiln and quality-critical functions on continuous coverage, while washing, some finishing activities and parts of dispatch can run with more limited shifts if inventory buffers are maintained.
12. CAPEX estimate and technology procurement

Core CAPEX is currently estimated at about 19,603,000 USD excluding optional SWRO and seawater systems. Optional resilience add-ons in the current line-item view are another 480,000 USD, but these are explicitly not recommended for phase 1.

The single biggest cost mistake at concept stage would be to look only at a kiln vendor's ex-works list price and mistake that for a real installed project cost. On an island brownfield, the final capital number is driven by buildings, civils, installation, electrical integration, controls, contingency and logistics almost as much as by the thermal core equipment itself.
Table 8. Concept CAPEX line items (abridged).
Figure 8. CAPEX by category.

Long-lead procurement should focus early on the kiln, optical sorting system, fine mill/classifier package and control architecture. These packages drive both lead time and process performance. Vendor RFQs should be issued before full civil commitment so that the basis of design remains aligned with real equipment footprints and services.
13. OPEX and base economics

In the integrated base operating case, including the ancillary-product branch, total modeled revenue is about 4,184,169 USD/yr and total OPEX about 2,795,588 USD/yr, producing EBITDA of about 1,388,582 USD/yr or 33.2%.

This is a workable but not invincible business case. The ancillary branch improves the headline numbers and should be included in the official model, but it does not remove the project’s dependence on local price realization and on keeping the factory fed. The conservative case remains much weaker, which means the project should only proceed after the commercial and feedstock gates are genuinely closed.
Table 9. Revenue and OPEX bridge by scenario.
Figure 9. Base-case integrated OPEX breakdown including ancillary direct cost.

The financial model should be interpreted as a concept-level decision aid, not as financing-grade certainty. Its job is to tell management where reality matters most. In this project, the most important sensitivities are product selling price, feedstock capture, and hidden brownfield cost. Water and desalination barely matter. Oversized heat-recovery hardware does not help. Tariff arbitrage does not save the battery case.

A simple 10-year unlevered model is included in the Excel workbook. Under the current base assumptions, a concept-level simple payback on core CAPEX remains relatively long, which is exactly why product-market validation and CAPEX tightening are mandatory before FID.
Figure 10. Scenario EBITDA comparison including ancillary branch.
14. Project risks and mitigation
The project is attractive precisely because it solves a real island problem. But it is not low-risk by default. The correct response is not pessimism; it is disciplined gating.
Table 10. Top concept-stage risks and mitigations.

Two risks deserve special emphasis. First, feedstock shortfall is existential. Second, hidden brownfield scope can quietly destroy returns without ever showing up in an optimistic concept note. Those two risks are why the development plan must start with contracts, pilot trials and due diligence rather than with procurement enthusiasm.
15. Recommended project phasing and gates
Table 11. Recommended project phases.
The project should not move to FEED or procurement until four pre-FID gates are satisfied:
Feedstock: signed LOIs / contracts above base raw-glass need.
Market: anchor customers covering the majority of base production.
Technology: pilot trials proving recipe and density window on actual local cullet.
Site / utility: brownfield and interconnection diligence confirming no hidden deal-breakers.
If those gates are closed properly, the plant can move into a rational 20–24 month implementation program. If not, more detailed engineering only creates a more expensive wrong answer.
16. Critical checklist
Table 12. Critical checklist before final investment decision.

This checklist should be used as an active project-management tool. Management should review it every month and refuse to let the project drift into procurement while core commercial or technical unknowns remain open.
17. Why the project is more compelling for government than for a pure financial investor

This project should be evaluated on two parallel scorecards: a commercial one and a public-value one. The commercial scorecard is fine. The public-value scorecard is strong. That difference needs to be explicit in both the detailed plan and the executive summary so that stakeholder expectations are set correctly.
Best institutional frame: government-backed PPP, utility-style SPV or development-oriented industrial platform with long-horizon capital.
Possible cooperation of friendly countries
Netherlands => Recycling topics are strong in whole EU
USA => Strong focus on building new hotels, boosting economy with local resources (ecology is aside, but still it covers their focus).
Another motivation for both can be that knowledge from this project can be used in other destinations too (possible partners France, UK for same reasons?)
Best private role: operator, EPC integrator, logistics partner, hospitality channel partner, local joinery partner or minority co-investor.
Worst framing: trying to sell the base case as a pure high-multiple venture-style return story. That is not what this asset is.
18. Final view

The Curaçao foam-glass project is technically credible and environmentally valuable, but only if it is built as a real industrial business and not as a romantic recycling concept. The project is small enough to fit the island, but not so small that discipline becomes optional.

The most encouraging result of the rework is that the plant's raw-glass demand is not inherently too large for Curaçao. The most important caution is that the margin between plausible island capture and plant need is not wide, so contracts matter.

The most useful engineering correction is that heat recovery and desalination must be right-sized rather than imagined. The project should explicitly avoid overbuilding utilities that have no true sink in phase 1.

My recommendation is to advance to the next step only through a short, focused pre-FEED work package: pilot trials on real cullet, feedstock LOIs, customer offtake interviews, brownfield/site diligence, and vendor RFQs for the kiln / optical sorter / mill / controls package. If those come back well, the project merits serious development.

Appendix C. Notes on the initial client concept note

The original client concept note is included in this project pack as an input document. This detailed business plan supersedes its first-pass estimates where necessary, especially for waste-heat utilization, water strategy, staffing realism and capex completeness.
Appendix D. Full scenario summary

The following table shows the broader scenario envelope used to test robustness. These scenarios are not equally probable; they are intended to show how quickly economics can move when density, front-end yield, energy intensity and renewable performance change together.
Table D1. Full scenario summary.

The critical takeaway is that the plant remains viable only when the commercial and technical base case is approximately achieved. In the conservative envelope, electricity cost and raw-glass demand both worsen at the same time, which is exactly what a stressed island operation can experience if contamination is high and thermal operation is unstable.
Appendix E. Operations, quality and maintenance concept

Because foam-glass quality depends on a relatively narrow process window, operations discipline matters more than in a simple crushing or washing line. Management should therefore define a small set of hard daily KPIs rather than a long list of vague sustainability metrics.
Table E1. Recommended operating KPIs.

Quality control should be embedded at three points: incoming cullet inspection, recipe preparation and post-kiln product testing. The plant does not need a research laboratory, but it does need a reliable operating lab for density, moisture, particle-size checks and simple strength / thermal-verification routines.

Preventive maintenance should be biased toward the marine environment. Corrosion, dust ingress and electrical connection quality are likely to cause more trouble on Curaçao than abstract 'wear and tear' averages from inland factories.
Table E2. Suggested maintenance rhythm.

A planned annual kiln stop should be designed into the business model. The current operating-fraction assumption already allows for significant downtime, but management should still define a formal stop scope and critical-spares list before commissioning.
Appendix F. Product inventory and dispatch concept
Table F1. Finished-goods inventory logic.

Even though finished-product mass is relatively low, finished-product volume is substantial. Warehouse and dispatch design must therefore prioritize cubic space, forklift circulation, bagging/pallet staging and weather protection rather than assuming that a small mass footprint equals a small logistics footprint.

For blocks, pallet pattern and protective packaging must be standardized early because freight damage can quickly erase the value of higher-margin product. For aggregate, the plant should preserve flexibility between bulk local truck dispatch and big-bag handling.
Appendix G. Why phase-1 desalination and large thermal storage are not recommended

This appendix exists because optional utilities are where concept projects often lose discipline. The best way to avoid that is to compare utility capex ideas directly against the scale of the real plant duty.
Table G1. Heat-recovery mismatch test.

If a 70 m3 hot-water store were built only to serve wash and dry, it would hold almost five operating days of the base thermal sink. That is a strong indicator that the storage volume has been designed from a generic idea of 'lots of kiln heat' rather than from the actual load profile.

The desalination case is even weaker. With process make-up water measured in only hundreds of cubic meters per year, a dedicated SWRO package would run at a tiny fraction of its practical capacity. That is operationally awkward and economically poor. Utility water with recirculation is the correct phase-1 answer unless external site conditions prove otherwise.

The right development question is therefore not 'Can we add desalination and large thermal storage?' but 'What proven phase-1 duty do they actually serve?' Until that answer is strong, those utilities should remain optional placeholders only.
Appendix H. Detailed CAPEX notes by package
The table below keeps the full line-item notes because management review often focuses on total capex only and loses sight of where uncertainty truly sits.
Table H1. Full CAPEX line items with notes.

The confidence labels are not decorative. They indicate where the project still needs price discovery. Brownfield civils, installation and process-critical custom packages deserve RFQs before any firm commitment is made on total project budget.
Appendix I. Suggested commercial workplan
The commercial workstream should proceed in parallel with engineering and should be owned explicitly rather than treated as a side effect of building the plant.
Map the top 20 likely local users of lightweight fill, insulation blocks and specialty aggregate and score them by purchase frequency, project size and likely openness to local recycled material.
Prepare a small physical sample set from pilot trials and use it in interviews rather than asking buyers to react to a concept description only.
Build a simple import-parity comparison for at least three product applications: lightweight fill, roof insulation build-up and non-structural insulation block use.
Offer early anchor customers a supply-assurance and local-availability story rather than a pure price discount story.
Coordinate the environmental narrative carefully: the project cleans the island and substitutes imported product, but the primary sale must still be technical performance and supply reliability.

A similar discipline is needed on the feedstock side. Hotels, bars and resorts should be approached with a service offer that reduces their waste-handling friction and provides visible ESG value, not only with a request for free glass.
Appendix J. Review summary for finance leadership

From a finance perspective, the most important strengths of this revised package are transparency of assumptions and explicit rejection of unsupported utility savings. The most important remaining tasks are to tighten market proof, feedstock proof and brownfield certainty.
Good news: plant scale is plausible for the island.
Good news: utility overbuild can be avoided.
Good news: own renewables materially reduce grid exposure without requiring full off-grid design.
Watch item: price realization is a major margin lever.
Watch item: front-end feedstock capture must be contracted.
Watch item: installed project cost still needs RFQ tightening.
In other words, the project deserves to move forward as a gated development program, not as a blind EPC rush. That is exactly the right profile for CEO and board-level review.
Appendix K. Ancillary products, lean CAPEX review, ABC platform and corrected diagrams

This appendix extends the original detailed plan, and it is kind of optional. The intent is to preserve the original depth and add the missing ancillary-product, regional-platform and lean-phase-1 content requested in review.
1. Integrated additions to the base plan

This integrated addendum keeps the base foam-glass concept but incorporates the previously omitted small products, corrects the logic of the factory diagrams, re-screens CAPEX for a leaner phase-1 build and frames the project as a potential ABC-islands infrastructure platform rather than only a stand-alone private factory.
Ancillary products are now treated as a formal micro-fab branch: artist packs, resin keychains, recognition plaques and limited-edition epoxy tables.

The preferred manufacturing route for the small products is bought-in plastic or acrylic preforms combined with epoxy/resin; for tables, casting can be done in-house while final wood or metal finishing is outsourced to a local joinery partner.
The CAPEX review removes day-one wind, BESS and full robotics from the mandatory base case while adding a compact tumble/cast/polish/packaging cell.

The strategic recommendation is now explicit: structure the project so it works for Curaçao alone, but actively design permitting, contracts and marine logistics so the plant can serve all three ABC islands.
Figure 1. Integrated scenario screen – Curaçao-only economics remain positive, while the ABC platform gives more headroom and resilience.
2. Product architecture – foam glass first, wow-products second

The commercial logic should stay simple: the factory exists to convert mixed waste glass into high-volume local building material. The ancillary products are intentionally small. Their role is to monetize the best-looking decorative fraction, improve project visibility, create lighter-workstation jobs and support hospitality, donor and CSR channels without distracting the plant from its core mission.
Foam-glass blocks/slabs Foam-glass aggregate / gravel
Figure 2. Foam-glass images carried forward from the original client input plan. These remain the core hero products.
Figure 3. Ancillary wow-products to include in both the detailed plan and the C-level summary.

The micro-fab branch should not justify heavy bespoke moulding equipment in phase 1. Standard bought-in preforms, simple vacuum/pressure casting fixtures, cure racks, polishing benches and packaging stations are enough to get to market quickly. For tables and other high-value statement pieces, the recommended route is to cast the glass/resin top in-house and complete the final structural finishing with a partner carpenter or metal fabricator on Curaçao.
3. Feedstock logic and ABC-islands recommendation

Modeled secured glass on Curaçao is about 3,427 t/yr. That is just enough for the lean 70 m3/day line, which requires about 3,451 t/yr of raw glass. In other words, the Curaçao-only case is viable but it has very little cushion. Once the plant is designed to receive material from Aruba and Bonaire, the secured regional pool rises to about 6,568 t/yr, which comfortably supports the 70 and 90 cases and makes the 105 case credible.
Figure 4. Secured feedstock pool by island. Aruba is the main strategic buffer once regional collection is activated.
Recommendation: permit and contract the project from day one so that it can legally and logistically serve the ABC islands, even if the initial operation starts with Curaçao material only.
At the 90 m3/day scenario, regional top-up equals about 1.08 containers per week. At the 105 m3/day screen it is about 1.87 containers per week, still manageable via short-sea logistics.

This regional framing also improves the project narrative for governments, tourism boards and development-finance stakeholders: one shared recycling asset, one shared building-material platform, one shared reduction in landfill pressure.
4. Process concept and corrected layout logic

The core factory remains a conventional mixed-glass cleaning line feeding milling, dosing and a continuous electric tunnel kiln. The corrected process and utility diagrams now show arrows only where a real connection exists. In particular, the energy sources now connect properly to the main plant bus rather than pointing into empty space.
Figure 5. Corrected process flow. The ancillary branch is a tiny selected fraction, not a second mass-production plant.
Figure 6. Corrected internal layout. Dirty, wet, hot and clean areas are now logically separated and connected.
Figure 7. Site masterplan with receiving yard, process hall, utility yard, dispatch and a small craft/showroom annex.

This matters commercially as well as technically: the ancillary branch only works if it remains subordinate to the core line. Color-rich decorative cullet should be picked only after cleaning and quality screening, so the plant never loses control of its main foam-glass throughput.
5. Utilities and resilience – phase 1 should be lean

The project concept recognizes the strategic value of renewable power, but the base CAPEX goes too far for a first build. The plant needs power resilience because the kiln cannot tolerate uncontrolled outages; however, it does not need every resilience feature on day one. The recommended phase-1 configuration is therefore PV plus grid tie plus diesel/UPS, with wind and BESS reserved as pads and interfaces for a later upgrade.
Figure 8. Corrected utility schematic. All arrows terminate on real systems; wind and BESS are explicitly shown as phase-2 options.
Figure 9. Lean phase-1 electricity balance at the 70 m3/day case. PV offsets roughly 43% of annual electricity use even before adding wind or storage.

Useful low-grade heat recovery is still attractive, but only at the scale of a small hot-water buffer for wash and dry support. The thermal opportunity is real, yet too small to justify exotic phase-1 infrastructure.
SWRO is not required for the base case. The water loop relies mainly on recirculation plus utility make-up water.
The lean build preserves upgrade optionality without forcing the project to carry optional systems inside the initial investment hurdle.
6. CAPEX review – reduce what is mandatory, keep options alive

The CAPEX review is intentionally practical. It does not assume heroic vendor savings on the core process. Instead, it asks which items are genuinely required for first operations and which ones can be reserved, prepared or staged for phase 2. That logic cuts phase-1 CAPEX by about $1.97m while still adding the small ancillary work cell.
Figure 10. Bridge from the full-scope concept CAPEX to the lean phase-1 CAPEX.
Wind turbine deferred: reserve electrical and civil interfaces only.
Battery storage deferred: keep EMS readiness, but do not force day-one spend before the plant operating profile is proven.
Robotics deferred: use manual or semi-automatic handling where safe and economically reasonable, then automate the real bottlenecks after ramp-up.
Ancillary micro-fab added: this is a low-cost, high-visibility workstation cluster and should remain small by design.
7. Economics – ancillary products help, but foam glass still carries the business

The economics are now presented as an integrated picture. The small-product branch adds about $361,200 of revenue and about $192,200 of EBITDA at only about 1.42 t/yr of curated glass use. That contribution is meaningful and should be modeled formally, but the big swing factors remain throughput, reliable feedstock capture, realized selling prices for foam glass and disciplined phase-1 CAPEX.
Figure 11. Revenue mix in the lean Curaçao 70 scenario.
Figure 12. OPEX structure in the lean Curaçao 70 scenario.

Read plainly: for a private financial investor, the 70 m3/day Curaçao-only case is not a knockout return. It is workable and strategically sensible, but not sensational. The case becomes more attractive once the regional feedstock pool is activated and the plant is treated as shared island infrastructure with local industrial-policy value.
8. Why the project is more compelling for government than for a pure financial investor

This project should be evaluated on two parallel scorecards: a commercial one and a public-value one. The commercial scorecard is fine. The public-value scorecard is strong. That difference needs to be explicit in both the detailed plan and the executive summary so that stakeholder expectations are set correctly.
Best institutional frame: government-backed PPP, utility-style SPV or development-oriented industrial platform with long-horizon capital.
Best private role: operator, EPC integrator, logistics partner, hospitality channel partner, local joinery partner or minority co-investor.
Worst framing: trying to sell the base case as a pure high-multiple venture-style return story. That is not what this asset is.
9. Recommended delivery sequence
Lock the 70 m3/day lean phase-1 design as the decision baseline and freeze optional systems as future interfaces, not immediate purchases.
Negotiate local supply and sorting contracts on Curaçao immediately, while in parallel preparing the ABC legal and logistics framework.
Prototype the ancillary products using bought-in blanks and local finishing partners before buying any custom mould tooling.
Pre-sell flagship table pieces, donor plaques and hospitality merchandise so that the wow-products launch with real reference customers.
Keep the business narrative honest: economically viable for Curaçao alone, strategically better and politically stronger as an ABC-islands project.

This plan therefore recommends a lean, first-build industrial plant with a deliberately small and photogenic craft branch. The ancillary products do not replace the foam-glass economics, but they do improve margin mix, visibility and political support. The plant should be designed to stand on its own on Curaçao, while being institutionally structured from the beginning as a shared ABC asset.

Why it matters for the islands
Local jobs across multiple skill levels
The core line creates industrial jobs, while the ancillary branch and partner joinery route add lighter assembly, finishing, retail and hospitality-linked work.
Foam glass can replace imported insulation or lightweight-fill material, improving regional supply resilience.
A functioning glass outlet reduces the stockpile footprint and gradually frees land currently occupied by low-value waste.
The wow-products provide visible proof that the islands convert waste into attractive objects and local value.
A shared ABC solution gives governments a concrete example of practical inter-island cooperation rather than another stand-alone pilot.
The project is not charity: it still has positive EBITDA and a route to payback, just with stronger public than purely private appeal.
